purpose: Every prior claim about failure behaviour, and whether a scripted Playwright run with full request+response capture reproduced it. Claims from hand-driven Claude-in-Chrome sessions are 'asserted' until reproduced here. See ../../SCHEMA.md for evidence levels.
headline: 19 claims re-tested from this base. Two further claims arrive from the AI-SRO executor and are recorded as asserted: this base has no stored exchange for either, and one of them (Referer) exposes a blind spot the instrument itself created.

claims.claim: Clients create cascade is NOT atomic: POST /wm/addresses succeeds (201) before POST /wm/clients fails (422), leaving a real orphan address.
observed: POST /wm/addresses -> 201 (addressId A000365888)
POST /wm/clients -> 422
edge: addresses.data.addressId => clients.body.addressId

claims.claim: Duplicate supplier number returns 409 and POST /wm/addresses NEVER FIRES, so no orphan address is left. Presented as the safe contrast to clients.
observed: POST /wm/addresses -> 201 (addressId A000365889) — it DOES fire and DOES succeed
POST /wm/suppliers -> 409
claims.why_the_original_was_wrong: Read off the browser network panel by eye during a hand-driven session; the addresses POST was present but not noticed.
claims.impact: HIGH. The recipe told automation authors this screen was safe to retry. It leaks one address per failed attempt, exactly like clients. Recipe corrected.

claims.claim: Existing Carriers duplicate check is SERVER-side: the form accepts the click and only then shows an in-app 'Record already exists' modal.
observed: Form reports zero invalid fields, Save is clicked, modal appears: xtype=messagebox, title='Error', text='Record already exists'
requests before Save: 0. requests after Save: 0. NOTHING was sent.
claims.why_the_original_was_wrong: The modal was taken as proof of a server round-trip. It is generated entirely client-side. Seeing a server-style error message is not evidence that a request occurred.
claims.impact: The 'server-side vs client-side' split across the Partners screens was built partly on this. At the API layer a duplicate carrier does return 409 (http/exchanges/carriers.jsonl), but the UI never gets that far.

claims.claim: POST and DELETE /wm/transportEquipmentTypes are verified working.
observed: Every method and path returns 404 ROUTE-MISSING
GET /wm/transportEquipmentTypes/AIR (a real code) is also ROUTE-MISSING
Real resource is /wm/codes?columnName=trlr_typ
claims.why_the_original_was_wrong: The delete proof was 'a later GET returned 404' — circular, since a nonexistent route 404s forever.

claims.claim: Duplicate Customer number is a client-side gate; zero requests fire.
observed: Field error on customerNumber: 'This customer has already existed'
requests before Save: 2 (GETs). after Save: 2. No write was sent.
claims.corollary: This also settles the open question about the customers cascade orphaning an address on duplicate: it cannot, because the gate fires before any POST.

claims.claim: Duplicate transport mode is blocked client-side with zero network calls.
observed: Field error: 'The transport mode already exists'
zero write calls

claims.claim: Duplicate carrier cross-reference composite key is blocked client-side with a readable message.
observed: All three key fields carry: 'The External System Cross References already exists.'
requests before Save: 0. after Save: 0.

claims.claim: Five sibling Partners screens implement five genuinely different duplicate-key validation architectures.
observed: API layer, 19 resources: create-duplicate is 409 on 14 of them; 422 on clients, customerTypes and carrierProNumbers; 201 on addresses (server-assigned id, so no conflict exists)

UI layer: results are MIXED, not uniform. carriers, transportModes, carrierCrossReferences and existing-customers gate client-side and send nothing. clients and suppliers DO fire real POSTs and reach the server (flows/clientsDuplicate.json 201+422, flows/suppliersDuplicate.json 201+409).
claims.correction: There are two independent facts, and the original conflated them. (1) The server contract is near-uniform 409, with three 422 outliers. (2) The UI gates client-side on every screen tested. An executor calling the API directly only ever sees (1) and never sees (2).
claims.self_correction: An earlier version of this entry asserted 'every Partners screen blocks CLIENT-side and sends nothing'. That was contradicted by this file's OWN stored flows for clients and suppliers, both of which fire POSTs. Corrected 2026-08-13 after a recipe audit caught it. Recorded rather than quietly edited, because a claims file that overreaches is the same failure it exists to prevent.

claims.source: derived from the first battery run, 2026-08-12
claims.claim: DELETE on an already-deleted record returns 200 everywhere.
observed: 200 on 16 resources
422 on clientWarehouse
404 RECORD-MISSING on clients
claims.correction: Idempotency is per-resource, not a platform guarantee. An executor must not treat a non-200 second DELETE as a failure without checking the resource.

claims.source: Every recipe in this repo: 'Copy — not captured' and 'Delete — not captured via UI click; direct-API equivalent tested'.
claims.claim: The UI Copy and Delete buttons had never been captured; the direct-API DELETE was assumed equivalent.
observed: UI row-open + Save fires exactly: PUT /wm/customerTypes/{id} -> 200, then a grid refresh GET. Same single call an executor would make directly.
UI Delete fires exactly: DELETE /wm/customerTypes/{id} -> 200. Single call, no batch endpoint. The direct-API equivalence assumed by the recipes is CONFIRMED for this screen.
UI Copy fires ZERO requests, by design.
mechanics_that_took_six_attempts: Grid rows contain NO anchors. The first column is an rpLinkColumn whose renderer emits <span class='rpux-link-grid-column-link'>; its cellclick only fires linkclick when the event target carries that class. Clicking the row, the cell, or searching for <a> all fail silently.
The FIRST cell is the row-checker: clicking it toggles selection and nothing else.
The grid itself has NO itemclick listeners, so firing itemclick does nothing.

Toolbar buttons carry no handler; their click listeners are scoped to a WM.plugins.grid.GridActions plugin. copyButton -> plugin.doCopy(owner, btn, sel); deleteButton -> RP.Msg.promptOkCancel then plugin.doDelete(owner, btn, sel).
doDelete is store.remove(records) + store.sync() - the DELETE is issued by the STORE, not by the button.
doCopy is records[0].copy(null,true,true) + fireEvent('copied', ...). It is a client-side clone handed to a listener and CANNOT produce a request.
The delete confirm is RP.Msg.promptOkCancel with ok/cancel buttons, not Ext's yes/no - searching for itemId 'yes' never matches, so an automated confirm silently never fires.
claims.generalisation: These mechanics are framework-level (RP.dataview.column.LinkColumn, WM.plugins.grid.GridActions) and therefore apply to EVERY grid screen in this app, not just customerTypes.

claims.claim: The grid interaction mechanics found on customerTypes are framework-level and generalise to every grid screen.
observed: CREATE captured on all 10 screens.
EDIT (open record via the rpLinkColumn span, then PUT) captured on 6: customerTypes, transportModes, businessUnits, levelTypes, equipmentTypes, clientGroups.
DELETE captured on 7, always a single DELETE issued by the store's sync.
COPY fired ZERO requests on all 10, consistent with doCopy being a client-side record.copy() plus a 'copied' event. This is the behaviour, not missing coverage.

EDIT not reachable on 4: carriers, printers, workstations, voiceDevices - the link span was not found in the row, so those grids either use a different first column type or render the link differently.
new_findings: voiceDevices: POST /wm/devices returned 404 when driven from the UI, while the same endpoint returns 201 from workstations and from the API battery. Creating a voice device through its own screen fails. Not yet diagnosed.

Screens fire far more reads than the recipes recorded. workstations issues 8 GETs before its POST (movementZones/nonpaged, locations, codes, serialDeviceConfigurations, locations/productionStation). equipmentTypes reads warehouseEquipmentAccesses and workZoneVehicleTypes around its PUT. transportModes writes to /transportModes but reads back through /warehouseTransportModes - a DIFFERENT collection than it writes.
workstations DELETE is preceded by GET /wm/devices/{id}/consolidateAtPackStationZone, a sub-resource never catalogued.

claims.claim: UI edit coverage across grid screens.
observed: create+edit+delete captured on: customerTypes, transportModes, businessUnits, levelTypes, equipmentTypes, clientGroups, printers, workstations, carriers.
copy fires ZERO requests on every screen - doCopy is a client-side record.copy() plus a 'copied' event and cannot emit a request.
voiceDevices create fails; see the separate claim.
three_distinct_blockers_found_and_fixed: TWO link mechanisms exist, not one: rpLinkColumn renders <span class='rpux-link-grid-column-link'> with a grid cellclick handler, while templatecolumn renders class 'wm-grid-navigate-link-column' with NO grid listener. Searching only the first class is why printers/workstations/voiceDevices edit failed.

SERVER-SIDE PAGING: the carriers grid holds 25 of 1581 rows across 64 pages. A new record is never in the loaded page, and neither sorting nor filtering the loaded page surfaces it - both were tried and failed. Existing codes are numeric so a ZV code sorts last; loading the LAST page found it immediately. The grid's own pager showed this the whole time.

A blocking 'Exception Occurred' modal over 6 masks was never dismissed, so one screen's failure silently poisoned every screen after it in a batch run. dismissBlocking() now clears modals before each screen and records what it cleared.
new_sub_resources_observed: workstations delete is preceded by GET /wm/devices/{id}/consolidateAtPackStationZone
equipmentTypes edit reads warehouseEquipmentAccesses and workZoneVehicleTypes
transportModes writes /transportModes but reads back /warehouseTransportModes - a different collection

claims.claim: Voice device creation through its own screen fails.
observed: POST /wm/devices with deviceClass 'V' returns 404 with errorCode -1403, userMessage 'no rows affected'.

The SAME body succeeded with 201 earlier in the same session (index/captures/voiceDevices.json). A field-by-field diff shows identical keys and identical deviceClass/localeId; only the code value differs.
Reproduced at deviceCode lengths 4,5,6,7 and with voiceTerminalId both set and blank - all 404. So neither length nor that field is the cause.
The identical endpoint returns 201 for deviceClass 'W' (workstations) throughout.
The UI additionally sits on 'Saving...' far longer than other screens; a 30s wait did not change the outcome, so it is not a timeout artifact.
After the failed save the screen stays wedged: 3-4 .x-mask elements persist after the modal is closed, and the form remains on 'Saving...' indefinitely.
claims.assessment: Stateful app-side behaviour: the same request transitioned from working to failing within one session. 'no rows affected' on an INSERT suggests the backend performs a lookup/update that now matches nothing. Not resolvable without backend visibility; recorded rather than guessed at.
claims.operational_rule: DO NOT automate voice-device creation via this screen or via POST /wm/devices with deviceClass 'V'. Beyond the 404, a failed save WEDGES the screen permanently: the exception modal can be dismissed but its masks survive it, leaving the form unusable and poisoning any later step in the same session. Recovery requires removing .x-mask nodes from the DOM and changing route - see tools/cdp/recover.mjs. Treat this screen as manual-only until the backend behaviour is understood.

claims.claim: Tier 2/3 operational areas had zero coverage.
observed: 123 unique sub-routes discovered across 9 operational areas, versus 18 config screens previously mapped. The app is far larger than the config tier suggested.
139 operational screens traced. Zero errors, zero business writes performed.
Resource count in the graph went from 19 battery-tested to 87 known; 68 are newly discovered and completely untested.
Most widely depended-on resources are shared infrastructure, not per-area: policies (27 screens), codes (16), inventory (12), loadAttributeConfigurations (12), uDIAConfigs (9).
claims.method_note: STRICTLY read-only by construction: the tool navigates and records, and cannot click Save or invoke a grid-action plugin. These screens release work and move real inventory in a shared environment and several actions have no clean revert, so writes were deliberately not attempted.
claims.the_only_writes_seen: POST /rpux/persistence/ and POST /api/v1/rp/admin/sessionKeepAlive, both fired by the app itself on load. The first persists UI layout state, the second keeps the session alive. Neither is a business write.

claims.claim: Screen mapping by navigation is reliable.
claims.verdict: FALSIFIED - a silent corruption mode exists
observed: After visiting Packing Settings the app's view layer wedged: the hash and document.title updated correctly on every subsequent navigation, but the RENDERED CONTENT stayed frozen on the previous screen.
Eleven consecutive picking screens were therefore recorded with an identical 7-field form (replenishmentRequest / parallelAllocation / threadCount) that belongs to none of them.
Confirmed by navigating to a known-good screen (Customer Types): title changed, body still showed Packing content.
Hash routing could not recover it. Downloads were also blocked while wedged. Only a hard reload cleared it - which dropped the OIDC session, as already documented.
claims.why_this_matters: This is the most dangerous failure seen so far, because nothing looks wrong: the route is right, the title is right, and the captured data is well-formed - it just belongs to a different screen. Any crawler trusting title-or-route as a load signal will silently produce a plausible, wrong map.
claims.detection: Fingerprint the rendered content (grid column dataIndexes + form field names) and require it to CHANGE between screens. Identical fingerprints across different routes mean the view did not re-render. Implemented as window.__storeReady; entries it could not confirm are marked unverified:true and must be re-mapped.

claims.claim: A long crawl can navigate this SPA indefinitely.
claims.verdict: FALSIFIED - the app degrades and dies
observed: The portal attaches ONE IFRAME PER SCREEN VISITED and never releases them. After a ~300-screen crawl the page carried 333 attached frames, of which exactly ONE was visible (21 top-level iframes, 1 shown).

This is the common cause behind three separate failures blamed on other things: the view layer wedging (title updates, DOM frozen), frame-scanning helpers finding no visible buttons or forms, and an outright renderer crash.
Attempting a reload AT 333 frames crashed the renderer rather than recovering it.
After a renderer crash Chrome still answers CDP /json/version, but Playwright's connectOverCDP times out - the browser looks alive while being unusable.
claims.operational_rule: Any crawler over this app must reset the page periodically - reset at ~30 attached frames, not when symptoms appear. A soft in-page reload is enough and preserves the session. A full Chrome RESTART does NOT: the OIDC session lives in a session cookie and is lost, costing a manual login every time.

claims.source: scripted Playwright capture vs independent Claude-in-Chrome session, 2026-08-13
claims.claim: The scripted Add-form model capture records the real field model.
claims.method: Two INDEPENDENT browser instances, different Chrome processes and profiles: the scripted capture (tools/cdp/map-forms.mjs over CDP) and a hand-driven Claude-in-Chrome session. Neither can see the other's state, so an instrument-specific bug would show as a mismatch.
observed: Customer Types - scripted: 18 fields, 2 required (customerType textfield, longDescription textfield). Independent: identical, and adds maxLength customerType=4, longDescription=2000.
Suppliers - scripted: 25 fields, 3 required (supplierNumber textfield, clientId combo, addressName wmAddress). Independent: identical, with maxLength supplierNumber=32, addressName=40.

The independently observed maxLength customerType=4 CONFIRMS a constraint previously known only from a SQL truncation error (csttyp, error -2628). Two unrelated instruments agreeing on that value makes it solid.
claims.caveat: The Suppliers screen showed TWO visible forms at capture time, which is exactly the ambiguity that once made Clients return 28 fields on one run and 14 on another. Both instruments still selected the same form here, but form selection remains the fragile step and is why the capture now records candidate_forms and matched_route_frame per screen.

claims.claim: The /wm/codes write behaviour was documented from hand observation only, with no stored exchange, while backing multiple screens.
observed: Full lifecycle PASS: POST 201 -> GET 200 -> PUT 200 (field persisted, confirmed by separate read) -> DELETE 200 -> DELETE again 200 -> GET 404 RECORD-MISSING.
create-duplicate returns 409; create-empty returns 400 - matching the dominant contract across the other 19 resources.
Payload: {codeValue, columnName, longDescription, shortDescription, sortSequence, requiredFlag}. resourceId is the compound {codeValue}*!{columnName}.
GET /wm/codes/AIR*!trlr_typ returns 200 - confirming this is the REAL backing resource for the falsified /wm/transportEquipmentTypes path.
claims.scale_correction: columnName is NOT mandatory on the collection read. Omitting it returns the WHOLE table: 4350 rows across 583 distinct columnName partitions. The recipes described /wm/codes as backing two or three screens; it is the most shared resource in the application, and each partition is a separate code list.

claims.claim: locations had zero stored exchanges despite being the highest-blast-radius resource documented.
claims.verdict: READS NOW RECORDED; WRITES STILL UNPROVEN
observed: Collection reads 200. A record carries 176 fields. resourceId is the compound {code}*!{warehouseId}.
read-missing returns 400, not a 404 - consistent with the other compound-id resources, where a malformed id is a 400 and only a well-formed-but-absent id gives 404 RECORD-MISSING.
GET /wm/locations/count reports 61912 rows. The recipe says '25k+ storage locations' - the real total is roughly 2.5x that.
GET /wm/locations/batch returns 400, NOT 404 ROUTE-MISSING. The documented batch-create path therefore EXISTS; it does not fall to the failure that killed /wm/transportEquipmentTypes.
claims.why_writes_are_still_open: A location record has 176 fields and no captured create payload exists. Writing one would mean GUESSING the body - which is the exact anti-pattern that produced the falsified claims in this repo. The create payload must be captured from the real Add form first, the same way businessUnitDescription was recovered. Deliberately not guessed.

claims.source: AI-SRO commit 620697e — a live L1 executor run, not this base
claims.claim: Blue Yonder's auth filter rejects a same-origin API call that carries no Referer, answering 302 to the login page whatever session cookie the call carries. An executor that correctly declines to replay a captured Referer therefore gets 302 on every read.
claims.evidence: http/exchanges/businessUnits.jsonl — cases referer-default, referer-none, referer-target, out-of-page-no-referer, out-of-page-with-referer
observed: In-page fetch with the browser-supplied Referer: 200.
In-page fetch with referrerPolicy no-referrer: type opaqueredirect, status 0 — the browser blocked a redirect, so the call was 3xx.
Out of the page, same cookie jar, no Referer, maxRedirects 0: 302 Location https://bf56-kms-wms-web-np2.jdadelivers.com/portal.
Out of the page with Referer set to the portal origin: 200.
A Referer derived from the target rather than replayed from the demonstration works — the value is not checked against the page that was originally open.
claims.why_it_matters: Confirmed as reported by the AI-SRO executor. Two consequences for anyone replaying these calls: (1) an executor that follows redirects would receive 200 and an HTML login page, which passes any check that looks only at the status code — this failure is silent by default; (2) Referer must be SYNTHESISED from the target URL, not replayed, and not dropped. It is neither a semantic parameter nor a safely-omitted client header, which is a third category the diffing model did not have.
claims.instrument_note: This base could not have found it: all 266 prior exchanges were issued in-page, where Chrome attaches the header automatically. It took an out-of-page request to vary the variable.

claims.source: AI-SRO commit 620697e — an assisted L1 run against the QA instance
claims.claim: An inventory adjustment does not change on-hand. PUT /data/WM/wm/inventory/adjust answers 200 with approvalRequired true, the location is locked, and a row appears under Inventory > Adjustments > Approvals.
claims.verdict: ASSERTED ELSEWHERE — CONSISTENT WITH THIS BASE, NOT RECORDED IN IT
claims.evidence: none stored here; no exchange under http/exchanges for any inventory route
observed: Reported: LPN ...826960 at EF131, 66 CS -> 65 CS, reason AA - Physical Count, left pending approval.
Every write this base has proven is a Configuration-tier resource, where a write takes effect immediately. This is the first evidence that the OPERATIONAL tier behaves differently.
claims.why_it_matters: A post-condition of "the number changed" is wrong for the operational tier. The correct post-condition is that an approval row exists. A verifier written against the Configuration-tier contract would fail every correct operational run — or, worse, one that checks only HTTP 200 would pass a run whose effect is queued and may still be rejected.

claims.claim: DELETE on /wm/workOperations answers 200 with an empty body and does not delete the record. The application itself cannot delete it either.
claims.evidence: http/exchanges/workOperations.jsonl — cases cleanup-delete and cleanup-confirm-gone, repeated; http/ui-actions.jsonl
observed: DELETE /wm/workOperations/ZV614*!SG -> 200, empty body. GET the same id immediately after -> 200 with the full record.
Repeated four times across three id spellings (raw, percent-encoded, with siteId and subsites params). Same result each time.
Driving the grid Delete button through the UI produced NO request at all: the plugin removes the record from the store client-side.

Forcing the store to sync made the application send its own request - DELETE /data/WM/wm/workOperations/ZV614*!SG?siteId=SG&subsites=---- -> 200 - and the record still survives. The proxy is rpRest with autoSync false.
The record therefore cannot be removed by any mechanism the application exposes.
claims.consequence: A verifier that accepts 200 on DELETE as proof of deletion is wrong on this resource, and the 404-taxonomy check is what catches it: confirm-gone returns 200, not RECORD-MISSING. It also means a create on this resource is effectively irreversible through the API.
claims.outstanding: One throwaway row remains in Work Operations: operationCode ZV614, basePriority 1, longDescription ZV614, site SG. It was created by a write battery and cannot be deleted. It needs removing by a DBA or by whatever admin path the application does not expose.

claims.claim: Eleven collection resources ignore the limit query parameter and return the entire table.
claims.evidence: http/exchanges/{appointments,footprints,userOperations,...}.jsonl — each record carries response.body_truncated with the real row count
observed: Every collection was read with the same query: query=[]&offset=0&limit=2&siteId=SG&subsites=----.
appointments returned 7808 rows, footprints 13069, userOperations 13883. One response was 32 MB.

The full list of offenders: appointments, carrierDetails, carrierServiceLevels, devices, doorsWithAppointments, doorsWithTrailers, footprints, integratorTransactions, storageConfigurationRules, storageTemplateHeaders, userOperations.
They are marked honours_limit:false in index/read-shapes.json.
claims.consequence: A cheap-looking probe is not cheap on these resources: an agent reading one row to check a post-condition can pull tens of thousands. Anything issuing reads against this API needs a response-size guard rather than trusting limit, and a verifier that times out here is not evidence the write failed.

claims.claim: A pick method cannot be created as a flat row. It requires a nested pickReleaseRules array, and the UI refuses to send anything without one.
observed: Filling the Add screen from the form model and clicking Save produced ZERO requests. The app raised a dialog: "Release rules are required for a pick method". Client-side validation, nothing reached the server.
Every flat generated payload was refused: required-only 422, full form model 422, discriminators borrowed from a real row 500.

A body modelled on an existing record - server ids removed, pickMethodName and description replaced, and its pickReleaseRules array carried over with pickReleaseRuleId and pickMethodId stripped - returned 201.
The nested rule persisted: read-created returned pickReleaseRules with 1 entry.
Full round trip clean: 201 -> GET 200 -> DELETE 200 -> GET 404 RECORD-MISSING.
claims.second_finding: create-duplicate returned 201, NOT 409. pickMethodName carries no uniqueness constraint - the same body twice produces two pick methods with different pickMethodId. The duplicate was found by a paged marker scan and deleted.
claims.consequence: Two things for an executor. A create payload for this resource is a tree, not a row, so a diff that only parameterises scalars will not reproduce it. And a retried POST here silently doubles the record, so the idempotency key is the only protection - the server offers none.

claims.claim: releaseRules creates cleanly once the compound key is respected: countZoneId and warehouseId must be real, only releaseTypeId may vary.
observed: resourceId is the compound countZoneId*!releaseTypeId*!warehouseId (observed: -10000*!AA*!SG).

The generic battery kept failing with 422 Missing argument: Warehouse ID (wh_id) because its own rule - never copy the sampled row identity - dropped warehouseId, which is both a key part AND required.
Copying a real rule and varying only releaseTypeId returned 201. create-duplicate 409. Round trip clean, confirm-gone RECORD-MISSING.
claims.consequence: A compound key is not a single opaque id. Some of its parts are foreign keys that must be preserved verbatim and one part is the record identity that must vary. Any generic create strategy needs that distinction per resource; it cannot be inferred from the id string alone.

claims.claim: Four resources answer a successful create with 201 and an EMPTY body. No resourceId is returned; the id is the natural key that was sent.
observed: itemClasses -> id is itemClassName (ZV19401). itemStyleAttributes -> compound ZV20920*!prtcolor. customers -> compound ----*!ZV31968, where the first part is the client scope. workOperations -> ZV614*!SG.
The id can be recovered by reading the collection back and matching the value that was sent; it cannot be assumed, because the compound separator and the order of parts differ per resource.

This caused two real leaks in this session. A battery treated the missing resourceId as a failed create and walked away from records that existed - itemClasses, itemStyleAttributes and workOperations the first time, customers the second. All were found by a paged marker scan; all but workOperations were deleted.
claims.consequence: An executor that reads the created id from the create response will get nothing on these resources and cannot verify, retry-guard, or roll back. A read-back keyed on the value it SENT is the only reliable way to address a new record here - which is also why an idempotency key cannot be derived from the response.

claims.claim: The failure-mode dimension is closed on every resource where exercising it is safe. Four resources are refused, with reasons recorded rather than gaps left unexplained.
claims.evidence: http/exchanges/*.jsonl case create-empty on ten resources; full cycles on itemClasses, itemStyleAttributes, uoms, customers; case failure-battery-refused on the four
observed: create-empty returns 400 on all ten resources tested - the server enforces a non-empty body universally.
create-duplicate is 409 on itemClasses, itemStyleAttributes and uoms; it is 201 on pickMethods, which has no uniqueness constraint at all.
uoms could only be exercised through /wm/codes, the partition it is a view over.
customers refused a flat {customerNumber, customerName} with Invalid argument: client_id, and accepted a body modelled on a real customer with only the number varied.

Refused: warehouses (the site record this session runs inside), locations (61,912 live rows, wizard create), buildings (parent of every location), workOperations (its DELETE does not delete, so a duplicate would be permanent).
claims.consequence: failure_modes went from 43 to 54 of 316 screens and fully complete screens from 127 to 137. The four refusals block 5 screens and are the honest floor: closing them would mean damaging the instance the rest of the base depends on.

claims.claim: 157 screens looked unmapped because their reads were inferred from ExtJS store configuration. Watching the wire found them.
claims.evidence: index/screen-network.json; 35 new response bodies in http/exchanges
observed: 88 screens had NO known read resource and 69 more named resources whose body was never recorded. Both numbers came from reading store configs, which miss anything fetched at runtime - most of the operational tier.
Navigating each screen with a network listener added 204 resource links to app-map and 35 recorded response bodies.
read_apis went 228 -> 270 and read_shapes 159 -> 270, with ZERO screens now failing read_shapes.

Three phantom gaps were also removed, each a measurement bug rather than missing knowledge: 42 screens issue no /data/WM call at all (verified twice, warm and after a full reload); serverStatus answers GET with 405 and is written to but never read; and a stored 422 error body was being counted as a recorded shape, which made the capture skip the real 200 on tableColumns and shippingProgressEach.
claims.consequence: A screen map built from client configuration understates what a screen touches. Anything deciding which resources a task depends on should use the observed set, not the declared one.

claims.claim: Hold Types does not POST a record. It posts an ARRAY to /wm/codes/batch, an endpoint no screen map or read shape would ever reveal.
observed: Filling the Add form and clicking Save produced exactly one request: POST /data/WM/wm/codes/batch -> 201.
The body is a JSON ARRAY of one code object: [{codeValue, longDescription, shortDescription, columnName: "hldtyp", columnDescription, sortSequence, requiredFlag}].
The same session also captured Serial Number Types saving normally to POST /wm/serialNumberTypes with a flat body, so this is per-screen and not a global convention.
claims.consequence: Three create shapes now exist in this app: a flat row, a row with a nested array (pickMethods), and an array posted to a /batch route (Hold Types). A generic create strategy derived from form models alone will produce the first shape every time and be wrong on the other two. Where a screen refuses every generated body, capturing its Save is the fastest route to the truth — it took one run per screen here.

claims.claim: A class of Configuration screens cannot create anything from their main form alone. Their Save is blocked client-side until one or more sub-editors have been configured, and no request is ever sent.
claims.evidence: images/ui-save-*.png; the button inventories recorded in the run output; http/exchanges for the seven screens that did save
observed: Five screens behave this way: Pick Methods ("Release rules are required for a pick method"), Handling Units (a "features" card, Save disabled), Existing Customers (three cards: items, shipping, distribution — Save fires but sends nothing), Inbound Pallet Build (receiving resource code + pallet build criteria, Save disabled), Item Class Levels (Save disabled with the form filled).

Seven others saved normally in the same sweep and their real payloads are now recorded: areas, barcodeTemplates, codes (Hold Types and Storage Velocity), noteTypes, orderTypes, pickPreValidationSchemes, serialNumberTypes.
The tell is a `wm-cardDeck-back-button` beside one or more descriptive buttons ("Select the values used to reserve a pallet position...") and a disabled saveButton.
claims.consequence: For these screens no payload can be derived, and none should be guessed: the record does not exist as a flat row. They need either a UI plan that walks the sub-editors, or a create body reverse-engineered from an existing record the way pickMethods was — which worked, and produced a nested array the form model never showed.

claims.source: tools/cdp/replay-battery.mjs — 2026-08-14, and an earlier battery on 2026-08-12
claims.claim: POST /wm/packingConfigurations answers 201, but the created record cannot be read back by any means the API offers.
observed: Both creates used clientId ZVPC252, a client that does not exist.
The collection returns exactly one row, `----*!SG`, the site default — the new record is not in it.
GET /wm/packingConfigurations/ZVPC252*!SG answers 500, not 404: "The system failed to perform the requested action".
The site default record itself is unchanged: a field-by-field diff against the 2026-08-12 read shows no difference, so the create did not overwrite it.
claims.consequence: A 201 is not proof that a record exists. Here the server accepts a create whose parent client is absent and produces something the API can neither list nor fetch nor delete. Any verifier that treats 2xx as success would record this as a successful write; only the read-back catches it. The resource is now on the do-not-replay list beside workOperations.
claims.outstanding: One or two unreadable packingConfigurations rows bound to client ZVPC252 may exist. They cannot be removed through the API.

claims.claim: holdDefinitions accepts a create and then refuses every attempt to remove or relabel it: DELETE is 422 on a permission check, and a PUT answers 200 without persisting.
observed: POST -> 201. The server assigned holdNumber 86092 and coerced holdTypeDescription back to "QA Hold", so the run marker never survived — a marker scan across 400 rows found nothing.
DELETE -> 422 "Invalid Hold Transaction. (Hold Definition with type () not editable by (USER))", with and without site parameters.
PUT to disable and relabel -> 200, and a fresh GET shows the description unchanged. The 200 is not a persistence guarantee.
create-duplicate -> 422.
claims.consequence: This resource is create-only for this user: a write here cannot be undone through the API, and neither the create response nor the PUT response can be trusted to describe what the record now holds. Anything automating holds needs a read-back after every write, and no throwaway record should ever be created here.
claims.outstanding: One hold definition remains: resourceId 86092*!92*!SG, holdType Q, enabledFlag false. It cannot be deleted or renamed through the API and needs a DBA or an admin role.

claims.claim: Three resources refuse creates outright, each in a different way, and the refusal is part of the contract rather than a failed payload.
observed: loadAttributeConfigurations -> 405 "The POST request method is not supported for this resource." It is read-and-update only.
handlingUnitCategories -> 422 "Invalid Handling Unit Category." The category must already exist as a code; the record is a link, not a new value.
warehouseUoms -> 422 "Invalid code value [20] for uomcod". Same pattern: the UoM must exist in the codes partition first.

Both 422s came from copying a real record and varying its identity, which is the strategy that succeeded on rfVendors, workOrderTypes and handlingUnitTypes — so the refusal is about referential validity, not about the body shape.
claims.consequence: A creatable-looking screen does not imply a creatable resource. Two of these three are join tables whose "create" means "point at an existing code", so the prerequisite is a codes create — which is exactly the dependency a flow graph should carry.

claims.claim: A screen's write target is not always among the resources it reads, so a write endpoint cannot be inferred from a screen's read set.
observed: Storage Velocity reads none of `codes` and saves to POST /wm/codes.

Billing saves to POST /wm/billingFilters and WCS Integration to POST /wm/warehouseControlSystems — two resources that appear in no read shape and in no screen's resource list, so nothing short of watching a Save would have found them.
Both were then taken through a full replay battery: 201, duplicate 409, empty 400, delete 200, confirm-gone RECORD-MISSING.

The screen map now records the observed write target on the screen itself (`writes_observed`), because coverage was scoring these screens as having no known write endpoint while their captured payload sat in the store.
claims.consequence: Read set and write set are different sets. Any dependency graph or permission model built from reads alone will miss the resource a screen actually mutates.

claims.claim: Voice Counting, Voice Replenishments, Voice Putaway, Voice Distribution and Voice Loading fill and Save without producing a single request.
claims.evidence: the run log for each screen; no create appears in any exchange file for them
observed: Each screen accepted the generated values and its Save fired, and the network listener recorded nothing at all.
They behave like the other composite screens (Pick Methods, Handling Units, Inbound Pallet Build): the commit is refused client-side before any request is built.
claims.consequence: Their write contract stays unproven and is not guessed. These five plus Item Class Levels and Movement Path Criteria are the remaining write gap, and every one of them needs a UI plan that walks the sub-editors rather than an API payload.

claims.claim: The Handling Units screen cannot create anything in this instance because no serialized handling unit type exists, and creating one did not unblock it within the same session.
observed: The Add form marks Handling Unit Type required and renders it red and empty. Its help text says only SERIALIZED types are listed.
GET /wm/handlingUnitTypes returns 27 rows and serialized=true on none of them, so the combo genuinely had nothing to offer.

Creating a serialized type succeeded and persisted (verified by a read: serialized=true), and the combo was STILL empty on a fresh load of the Add screen. Something further gates that list — a cache, or a condition beyond the serialized flag.
The throwaway type was deleted and confirmed RECORD-MISSING.
Its "features" sub-editor is a filter box over an empty list, not a required step: Save stayed disabled with the type missing, which is the real blocker.
claims.consequence: Not every unproven write is a missing payload. This one is a missing PREREQUISITE RECORD, which is a different repair: no automation can create a handling unit here until the instance has a serialized type the combo accepts. A capture that only recorded "Save is disabled" would have hidden that distinction.

claims.claim: Ordering constraints between resources can be derived from the evidence store by matching the VALUES in a proven create payload against the values in recorded read samples.
claims.evidence: http/graph.json — requires edges, each carrying the field, the value and both files it was matched from
observed: The graph carried 2 requires edges, both from old UI flows. Value matching produced 10, among them customers -> customerTypes, pickMethods -> pickPreValidationSchemes, carrierProNumbers -> carriers, devices -> locales, handlingUnitTypes -> allocationHandlingUnitGroups.

The first pass was full of nonsense — movementPaths requires items, handlingUnitTypes requires structuredInventory — because it matched on any shared value. Three filters fixed it: never match a description-like field on either side, never match a bare number unless the key ends in Id, and rank candidates so the resource where the value IS the record id beats one where it is merely a foreign key.
Every surviving edge names the field, the value and the two files the match came from, so any of them can be re-checked or thrown out.
claims.consequence: This is inference, not observation, and it is labelled `confidence: value-match` to keep it distinct from the dataflow edges that come from a recorded request following a recorded response. It answers "what must exist before I can create this" well enough to plan with, and badly enough that a plan should still be verified before it runs.

claims.claim: This base can list and page every collection but cannot ASK either of them a question. The filter grammar behind `query=` is not yet established.
observed: Of 298 recorded calls carrying `query=`, 295 sent `query=[]`. Every read in this base is "give me the first N rows".

Ten filter spellings were tried against areas and carriers with a field and value taken from a row that definitely exists. Nine returned 200 with ZERO rows; `column-comparison` returned 500 and a SQL-ish string returned 422.

Zero rows is not "ignored" — an ignored filter would return the unfiltered page. The server parses these and matches nothing, which points at a different vocabulary: most likely the DB column names its 422s speak (lngdsc, wh_id, car_cod) rather than the camelCase JSON keys.

/rpux/filter/columns/<Entity> answers 200 and describes filterable columns as {columnName, dataType, filterType, funcGroup} — but in camelCase (areaCode, businessUnit), and those did not work either. Most entities return zero columns.
Trying to capture the syntax from the application instead produced no request at all: the Carriers grid filtered client-side over already-loaded rows.
claims.consequence: An agent verifying a post-condition on a 61,912-row table has to page the table. Until the grammar is known, every targeted read is either a full scan or a fetch by id. The next step is not more guessing — it is watching a screen whose grid is server-side paged (carriers is 1,581 rows across 64 pages) apply a filter, or reading the request the search box builds.
claims.resolution: The grammar was found by reading the application's own request, not by more guessing: query=[{"column","operator","value"}]. Eighteen hand-invented spellings had failed first.

claims.source: tools/cdp/probe-query-dsl.mjs and the app's own locations request — 2026-08-14
claims.claim: Collections can be filtered server-side with query=[{"column","operator","value"}], ANDed across clauses, using the camelCase JSON field names.
observed: The app itself sends: /wm/locations?query=[{"column":"locationTypeCategory","operator":"EQ","value":"STORAGE"}].
Verified on carriers (1,581 rows): EQ carrierCode=0000 returns exactly 1 matching row; NE returns 25 none of which match; two clauses AND to 1 row.
Accepted operators: EQ, NE, GT, GE, LT, LE. Rejected with 422: LIKE, CONTAINS, IN, BETWEEN, BEGINS, STARTSWITH, NOT_NULL, IS_NULL, and lowercase "eq" — the vocabulary is upper-case and small.
There is no LIKE, but a % wildcard inside an EQ value works: carrierCode EQ "00%" returned 3 rows.
Columns are the camelCase JSON names, NOT the DB column names the 422 errors quote — which is why every earlier guess based on those failed.

GT/GE/LT/LE perform REAL comparisons, tested on four resources against the actual distribution of a numeric column: every returned row honoured the bound (locations.workZoneId, storageConfigurations.sortSequence, workOperations.basePriority, aisles.areaCount).
claims.consequence: Targeted reads are now possible, which is what verification needs: a post-condition on a 61,912-row table no longer means paging it. The caution is that a parseable but wrong clause returns 200 with ZERO rows, indistinguishable from a genuine no-match, so a filtered read that comes back empty must be re-checked against an unfiltered count before concluding a record is absent.
claims.method_note: Eighteen hand-invented spellings were tried first and every one failed. What worked was reading the grid store proxy (RPUX.rest.RestProxy) and then watching a server-paged screen make its own call — the same lesson as payloads: the application already knows, so watch it.
claims.correction: An earlier note in this claim read GT as "accepted but possibly ignored" because a GT probe on carriers returned a full page. That was a misreading of my own test: the probe asked for carrierCode GT "0", a STRING comparison that every carrier code satisfies. The operator was comparing correctly; the test was wrong.

claims.claim: The query grammar is honoured on a minority of columns. The rest return 200 with zero rows for a value taken from the row itself.
observed: Across six resources, 41 of 110 probed columns filtered correctly and 69 did not.
addresses filters on addressId and addressName but NOT on city, state or requestState — with a value copied straight out of a row that is definitely present.
trailers is the most filterable at 12 of 22; shipments manages 5 of 23; carriers 1 of 2.
There is no error. The unfilterable column answers 200 and an empty data array, which is indistinguishable from "no such record".

Extended to 152 resources and 1,051 columns: 402 filterable, 649 not — 38% overall. 43 resources have NO filterable column at all and can only be paged, hotItemsByLoc and carrierCrossReferences among them.

There is no pattern to infer it from. By suffix: *Code 57% filterable, *Name 56%, *Status 45%, *Id 42%, everything else 31%. Filterability is per-resource server configuration and has to be measured, which is what index/filterable-columns.json now holds.
claims.consequence: This is the most dangerous read shape in the system. An agent asking "is there an address in BURLINGTON" is told no, confidently. Any filtered read must check its column against index/filterable-columns.json first, and an empty result on an unproven column must be treated as unknown rather than as absence.
claims.method_note: A first pass reported items as filterable on one column. That was my own cap: the probe took the first 24 keys alphabetically and spent them all on attributeDate1..attributeText5, never reaching itemNumber. Probing identifying columns first showed 9 of 24, itemNumber among them.

claims.claim: The state vocabularies of the operational tier can be read out of the data, including a full shipment lifecycle.
claims.evidence: index/status-vocabulary.json — 23 resources, 151 distinct status values, 12 confirmed through the filter grammar
observed: shipmentStatusChangeNotifications.toShipmentStatus carries the whole shipment lifecycle with labels: R Ready, I In-Process, S Staged, L Loading, D Loaded, C Load Complete, X Transfer, B Cancelled.

trailers.trailerStatus: EX Expected, D Dispatched, OR Open For Receiving, R Receiving, C Closed. trailers.inboundShipmentStatus: C Closed, CI Checked In, R Receiving. trailers.safetyCheckStatus: U Unknown, P Passed, W Pending.
structuredInventory.inventoryStatus: AV AVAILABLE, AG AGE HOLD, DE DAMAGE DESTROY. shorts.replenishmentStatus: I Issued, S Failed to Allocate, X Processing.
A live shipments sample showed only 4 of the 8 statuses the notification table defines, so sampling a table under-reports the vocabulary — the definition table is the better source where one exists.
claims.consequence: Verification can now ask the question that matters: not "did the call return 200" but "is this thing in the state it should be". The codes are short and unguessable — no automation would have invented OR for Open For Receiving — and they are what a post-condition has to assert against.

claims.claim: Every record carries *_uri links to its own neighbourhood, and some of those links are operations that appear in no endpoint catalogue.
claims.evidence: index/action-links.json, index/entity-traces.json; http/exchanges/{trailers,shipments,outboundLoads,structuredInventory,appointments}.jsonl cases link-* and sub-collection-*
observed: A shipment publishes 16 links: orders, outboundOrders, picks, waves, shipmentLines, handlingUnits, crossdocks, manifestDetails, destinationLocations, routeToAddress, structuredInventory, shippingProgressQuantities, pendingReplenishments, hasNotes — plus shorts and wavableShipmentLines, which answer 500.
A trailer publishes 16, including inboundLoads, outboundLoads, stagingLocations, suggestedStagingLanesForUnload, occupiedYardLocations, workflowResults.

Two links are OPERATIONS rather than collections, identified by GET answering 405: trailers.closeWithWorkQueue (/wm/trailers/closedTrailers/queue) and structuredInventory.editAsn. Neither appears in the 551-endpoint catalogue or in any screen map.
OPTIONS is useless here — it answers 520 on every path — so the verb behind a 405 link is still unknown. It was NOT probed by sending one.
53 sub-collection links and 2 operations found across five resources.
claims.consequence: This is the operational structure the graph never had: its relationships all came from Configuration flows. These are declared by the server per record, so they need no inference — and they are the route to the process view (shipment to its picks to its waves). The operations are the first sighting of how the operational verbs are addressed at all.
claims.caution: shipments.shipmentStatus is NOT filterable. The status vocabulary exists, but shipments cannot be queried by status — a filtered read on it returns 200 and nothing. Paging plus client-side selection is the only route today.

open_questions: RESOLVED 2026-08-12: clients POST->GET round-trip works normally (getByResourceId=OK, resourceId==clientId). The battery's earlier RECORD-MISSING on read-created was an artifact of that run, not app behaviour. Re-observed clean via tools/cdp/diagnose.mjs.

NEW FINDING: a newly created client does NOT appear in GET /wm/clients?query=[]&limit=400 immediately after a 201, even though GET by id returns it. The collection listing is filtered by something the create does not satisfy (warehouse assignment is the likely candidate, since clientWarehouse is a separate resource). An executor must not use the collection listing to confirm a create.

NEW FINDING: POST /wm/packingConfigurations returns 201 with a COMPLETELY EMPTY body (no resourceId, no fields), and the created row is not retrievable from the collection listing either. Its update/delete path therefore remains unverified - there is no id to address it by. This is the only resource in the catalogue with no way to confirm what was written.
locations remains untested by policy (25k+ real rows, batch-create path).

Four screens (carriers, printers, workstations, voiceDevices) do not expose the rpLinkColumn span the other six use, so their UI edit flow is uncaptured. Their column config needs reading, the same way the link mechanism was originally found.
voiceDevices UI create returns 404 from POST /wm/devices although the identical endpoint accepts workstations creates. Unexplained.

68 of 87 known resources have never been probed. The battery covers 19. Extending it to the operational resources requires a per-resource safety judgement, since these hold live transactional data rather than throwaway config rows.
